title: Iran Warns Ukraine of Retaliation After Caspian Ship Attack as Rosneft Says China, Not OPEC, Calls the Shots
subhead: The US-Iran pause held for a third night, sending Brent below $90, even as Iran insisted it still controls the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile the conflict opened a new theater — Iran accused Ukraine of a deadly Caspian Sea strike — and Rosneft's CEO argued China, not OPEC, now sets the oil market's direction.

sections.heading: US-Iran Pause Holds as Oil Plunges Below $90
sections.body:
The US and Iran held fire for a third consecutive night, and oil prices paid the price of de-escalation hopes. Brent crude fell below $88 a barrel — down more than 9% — while US crude dropped to around $83, roughly 7% lower, according to BBC and NBC News. The slide came after Trump paused 13 consecutive nights of strikes and Iran halted retaliatory attacks to open diplomatic space.

Yet Tehran pushed back on the premise of talks. Iran said it still controls the Strait of Hormuz and is not seeking new negotiations with Washington, per Reuters, leaving global shipping routes in limbo. In parallel, Iran and Oman advanced an 'interim framework' for a temporary joint shipping corridor through the strait, with Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi saying both sides agreed on a temporary route and aim to negotiate a permanent corridor within 30 to 60 days, OilPrice.com reported. Oil loadings from Iraq's Persian Gulf terminals surged at the start of the week, with satellite imagery showing seven tankers collecting cargoes — one of the clearest signals yet that Gulf producers expect tensions to ease.
sections.whyItMatters: The pause is real but fragile: Iran publicly rejects talks even as its diplomats negotiate a corridor with Oman. The market is pricing a partial reopening of Hormuz, but Tehran's rhetoric and the still-blocked strait mean the war premium could return quickly.

sections.heading: New Theater: Iran Accuses Ukraine of Deadly Caspian Strike
sections.body:
The US-Iran conflict acquired a second front. Iran accused Ukraine of attacking an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea on July 25, killing one sailor and wounding another, Anadolu Agency reported. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned the attack 'cannot go unanswered,' escalating tensions beyond the US-Iran war into a new theater.

Iran went further, accusing Israel of provoking the strike to drag Europe into a wider conflict, according to Al Jazeera. The accusation lands as Ukraine and the US coordinate a new peace push with Russia, and as Kyiv expands deep-strike operations — including drone attacks on Russian oil infrastructure in Rostov, Udmurtia and Yaroslavl, per the Kyiv Independent.
sections.whyItMatters: A Caspian Sea attack on Iranian shipping, if confirmed, would pull Ukraine into the Gulf war's orbit and complicate the US-Iran pause. It also shows how the conflict is radiating beyond the Strait of Hormuz into new maritime theaters.

sections.heading: Saudi Oil Infrastructure Under Drone Attack
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia's oil facilities came under renewed attack even as the US paused its bombing of Iran. Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed drones launched from Iraq by Iran-backed militias targeting the kingdom's petroleum facilities, the New York Times and CBS News reported. Yemen's Houthis separately claimed drone strikes on Saudi crude oil transport infrastructure, per France 24.

The attacks are testing the fragile ceasefire. Red Sea shipping slowed after Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations, with ship traffic through Bab el-Mandeb falling while Strait of Hormuz transit stayed low over the weekend, Reuters reported, citing Kpler shipping data.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran's proxies are probing the pause's limits by striking Saudi energy assets without direct Iranian involvement. This keeps the Gulf's oil infrastructure in the crosshairs even as Washington and Tehran hold fire, and it is throttling Red Sea shipping independent of Hormuz.

sections.heading: Rosneft CEO: China, Not OPEC, Calls the Shots
sections.body:
Russia's top oil executive delivered a blunt reassessment of who actually steers the global oil market. Igor Sechin, CEO of Rosneft, said China — not OPEC — is now calling the shots, arguing Beijing has 'taken the initiative from OPEC' by acting as the ultimate swing buyer, OilPrice.com reported. Speaking at an economic forum in Vladivostok, Sechin said China stabilized the market by slashing crude imports by about 5.5 million barrels per day without joining any cartel.

Sechin's argument rests on China's stockpile cushion: the world's largest crude importer had amassed an estimated up to 1.4 billion barrels in commercial and strategic reserves before the Iran war, allowing it to cut imports sharply and absorb the shock of the Hormuz disruption.
sections.whyItMatters: A Putin ally publicly declaring that Beijing, not the cartel, now sets the market's direction is a significant signal. It reframes OPEC's power and underscores how China's reserve policy — not Saudi or Russian output decisions — has been the real shock absorber during the Iran war.

sections.heading: US Strategic Petroleum Reserve Nears Critical Levels
sections.body:
The emergency cushion that helped contain oil prices during the Iran war is running thin. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve could fall to around 243 million barrels, below the level considered optimal for efficient operation, OilPrice.com reported. Heavy SPR releases have been central to the OECD's coordinated response, which included a controlled release of 400 million barrels.

Refilling the reserve is proving difficult: Venezuelan heavy crude may not be suitable for SPR infrastructure designed primarily for lighter grades, complicating any plan to replenish stocks with discounted Venezuelan barrels. Dwindling US and Chinese inventories are reducing the market's emergency supply cushion just as the Gulf crisis drags on.
sections.whyItMatters: The SPR was the market's shock absorber during the war. With it near critical lows and refill options limited, the US has far less firepower to blunt the next price spike — a structural vulnerability if Hormuz stays blocked or the war re-escalates.

sections.heading: US, Japan and South Korea Forge a Nuclear Alliance
sections.body:
Northeast Asia is folding energy policy into trilateral security cooperation. The US, Japan and South Korea signed a trilateral small modular reactor (SMR) cooperation agreement in July to give countries an alternative to Chinese and Russian reactor vendors, OilPrice.com reported. Japan and South Korea are ramping up nuclear expansion and syncing it with Washington as part of their energy security strategies.

The push is being accelerated by AI-driven power demand and fossil fuel supply disruptions from the wars in Russia and Iran, which are driving a global nuclear revival. The trilateral deal positions the three allies as a counterweight to Beijing and Moscow in the reactor export market.
sections.whyItMatters: Nuclear reactor diplomacy is becoming a great-power competition arena. A US-Japan-South Korea SMR bloc directly challenges Chinese and Russian reactor exports, turning civilian nuclear technology into a strategic tool in the same way energy infrastructure already is.

sections.heading: UK Closes the Russian Crude Fuel Loophole
sections.body:
London has put a date on closing a sanctions loophole. The UK will ban imports of diesel and jet fuel refined from Russian crude in third countries no later than January 1, 2027, OilPrice.com reported. The move builds on May sanctions prohibiting refined oil made from Russian crude, but closes the temporary license that had allowed Russian crude to be shipped to a third country, refined there, and re-enter the UK as fuel.

Officials said the current license is subject to review every two weeks and could be terminated earlier if market conditions allow, with industry receiving at least four months' notice before any changes take effect.
sections.whyItMatters: The UK is targeting the backdoor routes that blunt Western sanctions on Russian energy. Closing the third-country refining loophole tightens the squeeze on Russian crude revenue, though its impact depends on whether other buyers and refiners step in to absorb the redirected flows.

bottomLine: The US-Iran pause held for a third night and sent Brent below $88, but the de-escalation is fragile: Iran publicly rejects talks even as it negotiates a Hormuz corridor with Oman, its proxies keep striking Saudi oil infrastructure, and the conflict opened a new theater with Iran accusing Ukraine of a deadly Caspian strike. Beneath the price action, two structural shifts stand out — Rosneft's CEO declaring that China, not OPEC, now steers the market, and the US SPR nearing critical lows with limited refill options. The market is betting on a partial reopening of Hormuz, but the war premium could return quickly if the pause collapses.
sources: BBC, NBC News, Reuters, Anadolu Agency, Al Jazeera, New York Times, CBS News, France 24, Daily Sabah, AP News, Kyiv Independent, Stars and Stripes, LA Times, OilPrice.com, ZeroHedge
